Québec (Procureur général) c.
Académie Yeshiva Toras Moshe de Montréal

2011 QCCS 4622

JG2163

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

MONTREAL

No.:

September 7, 2011

______________________________________________________________________

PRESIDING:

THE HONOURABLE

GÉRARD DUGRÉ, J.

______________________________________________________________________

ATTORNEY GENERAL OF QUEBEC

plaintiff

v.

ACADÉMIE YESHIVA TORAS MOSHE DE
MONTRÉAL

- and -

JACOB JOËL MAMAN

- and -

HERSCHEL LOWY

MONTRÉAL

MARGUERITE-BOURGEOYS

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

I.

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

The Attorney General of Quebec (the
"Attorney General"), representing the Quebec Minister of Education,
Recreation and Sports (the "Minister"), seeks orders for
interlocutory injunction to require the defendants, more specifically the
Académie Yeshiva Toras Moshe de Montréal (the "Académie") to cease
operating an educational institution dispensing elementary and secondary
educational services to school age children within the meaning of
section 14
of
the
Education Act
[1]

(the "
E.A.
"),

while permitting religious
extracurricular activities to be carried on without restriction.

[
2
]

The Attorney General maintains that the Académie
is a private educational institution subject to the
Act respecting Private
education
[2]

(the "
A.P.E.
") and that, consequently, the Académie is
infringing section 10 of that Act because it does not hold a permit issued by
the Minister for the institution and for the educational services it dispenses.

[
3
]

The defendants, and the Académie in particular,
vigorously contest this motion. They argue, among other things, that the
Académie is not subject to the
A.P.E
., that the tests for issuing an
interlocutory injunction are not met, and that the discretionary nature of
injunctive relief, particularly at the interlocutory stage, requires that the
orders sought in this case not be issued.

[
4
]

It should be noted that the defendants have
brought a counterclaim seeking,
inter alia
, a permit granting them the
exemptions set out in
paragraph 2
of
section 22
of the
Regulation respecting
the application of the Act respecting private education

(the

“
Regulation
”)
.
[3]

[
5
]

After having heard the parties, analyzed the
abundant documentation submitted, and on the whole deliberated, the Court
finds, for the following reasons, that the orders of interlocutory injunction
sought in this case should not be granted. Therefore, the Attorney General's
motion for interlocutory injunction is dismissed.

II.

THE PARTIES

[
6
]

The Attorney General represents the Minister,
whose responsibilities include the application of the
A.P.E.
and its
regulations.

[
7
]

The Académie, which has been providing
educational services to boys in the Satmar Chassidic community since 1952, was
constituted under Part III of the
Companies Act
[4]
on December 7, 2000.

[
8
]

The defendant Jacob Joël Maman is the director
of secular studies at the Académie. The defendants Herschel Lowy, David
Meisels, Abraham Drummer, Alexander Fried, Israel Mendlovic, Martin Oberlander,
and Sydney Lebovits are, among other things, its administrators.

[
9
]

To properly understand the social, religious,
and legal issues raised by the plaintiff's motion for interlocutory injunction,
we shall reproduce excerpts from the expert report prepared by Dr. Thomas
Kessner, Professor of History at City University of New York.  His report
[5]
explains the history,
demographics, and religious beliefs and practices of the Satmar Chassidic
community to which the 163 children who attend the Académie belong.

By means of this report I hope to
give the Court some insight into the history, demographics and core religious
beliefs and practices of the Satmar Chassidic Jewish community, and situate the
Montreal community among the various Satmar communities worldwide. ...

Chassidic Judaism

Like most Chassidic groups the
Satmar community traces its roots to the origins of modern Chassidism in the
eighteenth century. The movement arose in troubled times, amidst violent
pogroms, oppressive taxation and discriminatory laws that barred Jews from many
common trades, crafts and occupations. In some countries they were prevented
from voting and from settling in specified regions and cities. Entire countries
closed their doors to Jews, while others restricted their habitation to
unwholesome ghettoes. In general, this many-stranded noose of restrictions made
them citizens as to obligations but aliens as to rights.

In this environment many Jews
welcomed the stirring message of Chassidic leaders who, drawing upon Jewish
traditions in Talmud, Halacha (practical law) and Aggada (ethical parables,
maxims and traditional wisdom), emphasized the value of living a committed
life, praying with zeal, doing simple good works and acts of human kindness; of
living a life uplifted by a serene notion of Divine immanence as an alternative
to the more exclusively scholastic approach prevailing before that time. These
goals placed legitimate religious achievement and success within the reach of
common people and not just within the restricted precincts of the intellectual elite.
The notion that one could attain a consecrated life through humble sincerity,
joy in the fulfillment of commandments and in following the word of G-d, even
if full understanding remained elusive, exerted a huge attraction and helped
spread the Chassidic message. Emphasizing the mystical chords that connected
the souls of the common folk with their Creator, this populist movement placed
a direct and authentic relationship with Hashem (their way of referring to G-d)
within reach of all, including the poor and unlearned. Every person could wield
a cosmic influence with his behaviour.

It must be borne in mind however
that Chassidic teaching did not alter the basic framework of Torah life, shaped
by the imperatives of revealed doctrine. It did not challenge or modify the
sacred canon. Like all Orthodox Jews, Chassidim believe that the Torah, the
five books of Moses, is the literal word of G-d and that carrying out this word
is what gives meaning and purpose to life. For Orthodox Jews, this means
following all of the 613 commandments found in the Torah that are still
practicable. These positive and negative commandments govern ritual and ethical
obligations, defining the individual’s relationship to G-d and to Man. They
govern conduct in everything from giving charity to not mixing wool with linen,
from keeping dietary laws and refraining from work on the Sabbath, to studying
the Torah and loving and fearing G-d.

Under the influence of charismatic
Grand Rabbis (Rebbes) the movement gained wide popularity in Poland, Ukraine,
Lithuania and eventually Hungary and Romania. By the eve of World War II,
Chassidism, recognized as part of normative Orthodox Judaism, boasted millions
of followers.

Then this world was plunged into
darkness. The Holocaust wiped out much of European Jewry along with their
institutions and their spiritual centers. From 1939 to 1946, Chassidic
religious and communal life all but ceased, persisting often heroically in the
nooks and crannies of concentration camps and hiding places. A tiny vestige,
ragged and demoralized, survived and ultimately sought refuge in North America*
(*Yaffa Eliach, in
Hasidic Tales of the Holocaust, tells of one of the
Chassidic Grand Rabbis arriving in New York City in 1946
...)

Rabbi Yoel Teitelbaum and the
Satmar Community

The present Satmar Chassidic
community in North America consists primarily of the descendants of Eastern
European survivors of the Holocaust who came to this continent following World
War II. The Satmar name comes from the town of Satu Mare, which is currently in
Romania, but was also under Hungarian control for a period of its history.
Today the largest concentration of Satmar Chassidim can be found in New York
State, where estimates place their numbers at upwards of 100,000 individuals.
Satmar communities can also be found in Los Angeles, Montreal, Buenos Aires,
and overseas in Antwerp, London, and Manchester as well as in Australia and
Israel.

The original group of post-war
survivors was led by Rabbi Yoel Teitelbaum (1887-1979), and descendant of Rabbi
Moshe Teitelbaum (1759-1841) who introduced Chassidism to Hungary. Chassidim
were accustomed to taking direction on every important aspect of their lives
from their Rebbes, the holy men whom they looked up to. Now after the war they
sought leadership and guidance more than ever before. They rallied around Rabbi
Yoel Teitelbaum who had served as a communal rabbi and headed the Talmud
Academy in Satu Mare before the war. Even then he was revered for his
brilliance, his mastery of Jewish scholarship and for his extraordinary piety
and unswerving allegiance to traditional practice and outlook. Now, refusing to
yield to the prevailing despondency after the Holocaust, Rabbi Yoel gathered
the broken men and women around him and insisted to them that there had once
been a world built around their better dreams and that they must build it anew.

On his narrow shoulders the Satmar
Rav, as Rabbi Yoel came to be known, lifted up an orphaned generation and
sparked in them the courage to look to a new future beyond despair. From the
scarred survivors of the Holocaust he erected a vibrant new community in the
United States. Some argued that he ought not expect too much, nor push too
hard, after all he must make accommodations to the new environment. In the
United States the dress and manner of Chassidism was alien and these advisers
suggested that modern life demanded a lower profile and a lesser religious
practice. To them he replied forcefully that truth did not change with time and
place. If the effort to replant Chassidic Judaism in the New World was to
succeed it must be built on the firmest of foundations. It was not at all clear
that such an unbending position would succeed, but he refused to accept the
idea that undiluted Judaism had no future. To the contrary, he insisted that
the power of Torah principles was that they were eternal – twisting them to
meet the mood of changing times would only wear away their truth and their
beauty.

Others had failed in the past to
establish a vibrant Jewish Chassidism in North America. Undeterred, he inspired
his followers to aspire to a future that was true to their past. If only
judging from the present vitality of the Satmar communities in the world, one
can observe that Rabbi Yoel’s leadership accomplished many of these goals. He
nourished his flock, taking a hand in their every problem, giving them courage
and the wherewithal to succeed in fashioning new lives. He encouraged them to
marry, build communities, and aspire to raise a new generation. At the same
time that he led his flock and built for the future he pursued a remarkable
career as a scholar and thinker whose influence reached well beyond the
confines of the Satmar community. His long list of influential books and
lectures provided the intellectual underpinnings for a new generation of
Chassidic Judaism. He also helped develop the communal infrastructure for
future growth, leading his Chassidim to build charities, social organizations,
communal agencies and fraternal institutions. At the core of this communal
infrastructure he placed a school system, a system for the post-Holocaust
generation and for the generations to come.

In the course of five decades the
modest one room school in Brooklyn’s Williamsburg section with which he began
gave rise to a worldwide school network from pre-school through advanced post
graduate levels with branches in Borough Park, Monroe, Monsey, Lakewood,
Montreal, Jerusalem, Buenos Aires, Bnei Brak, Antwerp, London and Manchester.

The Importance of Education
for the Satmar Community

The values of the Satmar community
remain distinctive, forming a part of the diverse modern world and interacting
with it. Satmar Chassidim work side by side with their fellow citizens. They
vote and they make important contributions to business, politics, civic life
and national culture, but at the same time they shelter their children from TV,
internet and other vehicles of a mass culture that they feel has lost its
regard for restraint and respect for tradition. They reject exhortations to
‘live for the moment,’ and aim to protect their youth from a consumer culture
that they believe exquisitely packages every conceivable form of temptation.
They insist that children (and adults too) need to be shielded from
entertainments that stir up their lowest instincts.

The congregational community has no
walls and there are no guarantees, but the Satmar community places its faith in
education, in creating a rationale for distinctiveness, based on Torah values.
They understand however that a sub-culture cannot persist unless it has the
intelligent ability to explain itself to its children and that to educate a
generation in the contemporary world it is critical to raise all the important
questions and address them.

To this imperative they bring
experience with a system of education that traces back thousands of years to
the Talmud Academies of ancient times. Two thousand years ago Rabbi Yehoshua
ben Gamla, insisting that schooling was a communal responsibility, saw to it
that a network of Torah schools were established in each region that was under
Jewish control. Under his insistent leadership schooling was made universal and
paid for by the community. Over the many centuries of the Jewish Diaspora, the
transmission of cultural memory and understanding has occupied the vital center
of Jewish life. Wanderers of the globe, the Jewish people have interacted with
many cultures, lived among the nations, and borne with pride and commitment a
treasure of learning that bound them together as a people for more than 3,000
years. Commanded to a sanctified life by the revealed law, they studied this
law for every nuance and applied its unvarying rules to swiftly changing
environments.

Even today by the age of five,
Satmar children spend an entire day in school, learning to read in several languages
and studying history, ethics and the Bible. In the afternoon they turn to
studies of language, math and grammar. By the time these children are nine or
ten, girls pursue a diverse syllabus of studies, while their brothers spend
much of each morning and early afternoon studying the complicated case texts of
the Talmud. Young boys, whose experience with farm animals is limited to the
petting zoo, participate in theoretical discussions assessing responsibility if
a calf walking through the public square kicks a pebble that breaks a window,
or topples a lantern causing a fire. At the age of nine they are studying
Talmudic tort law, only they are studying it in the original texts that were
composed in Hebrew and Aramaic thousands of years ago. We are not talking about
honors students or elite academies for the select few. This is the conventional
Yeshiva education: children making close readings of classic texts while they
are urged on to challenge the reasoning and ask good questions, and to point
out apparent inconsistencies and curious bends in the Talmudic logic.

The Satmar community places much
emphasis on maintaining pre-war traditions and they have established a school
system along traditional lines. To better understand this position it is
worthwhile to consider historical experience. One example: in Czarist Russia in
the 1840s the Minister of Public Education, Sergei Uvarov, established a
committee to reform Jewish schools. He inveigled Max Lilienthal and other
Jewish figures into supporting this scheme and then foisted it upon the larger
Jewish community, appointing individuals who then sought to undermine the
entire system of Jewish education. Rabbi Yoel’s own father waged a fierce
campaign in pre-war Marmarosh (Romania) against state imposed schooling for
precisely this reason. For these and other related reasons the Satmar community
is extremely sensitive over the autonomy of its schooling. It has willingly
paid the price for a private school system in order to shape the transmission
of its religious values without undue interference. At the same time, Chassidic
schooling promotes many of the values which are those of the society at large.
Students are encouraged and trained to become law-abiding citizens with a deep
sense of loyalty and appreciation for the rights and privileges that
citizenship affords them.

The Satmar school system’s teachers
of Talmud are generally drawn from their own community. While these instructors
do not hold conventional university degrees, virtually all have graduated from
AARTS- (Association of Advanced Rabbinical and Talmudic Schools) approved
college and university level schools. In the United States AARTS is recognized
by the Department of Education as an accrediting agency for post secondary
level schools and its schools offer degrees which in some states are Bachelor’s
and Masters Degrees and in other states are First and Second Talmudic Degrees.
These degrees are based on a long period of training for such fields as
teaching Talmud and related professions.

The results and outcomes of this
schooling have been quite impressive. Leaving aside the intellectual and
cultural outcomes, which it may be argued are difficult to assess on a
universal scale Satmar people have achieved a fair amount of material success.
They are entrepreneurs in such areas as the diamond industry, import-expert and
manufacturing. They serve as computer consultants, electricians, and building
contractors and work in offices, factories and retail shops. Many are involved
with providing goods and services to their own community, teaching, processing
and distributing kosher food items, religious articles, publications and
Chassidic clothing. Yet others are involved in the garment manufacture and in
retail electronic sales. Satmar spokesmen point with pride to the fact that in
each country where they live the Satmar community has made solid contributions,
served as constructive citizens and achieved economic stability. Furthermore,
the incidence of crime in their communities compares favorably with the population
at large. In New York City where the police publish precinct level crime date,
the heavily Satmar and Chassidic Borough Park Community District ranked 59
th

of all 59 Community District for the incidence of felony crimes per thousand in
year 2007.

Other Aspects of Satmar
Chassidism

The Satmar Chassidic movement is
also famous for its many charitable organizations, which were founded by Rabbi
Yoel Teitelbaum and his wife, Rebbetzin Alte Feiga Teitelbaum. The Satmar
Bikur
Cholim
helps care for the ill in hospitals and provides assistance for
needy families that require help with paying for medical treatment.
Rav Tov

was founded originally to help Jews in the Soviet Union. Now it helps refugees
from such lands as Iran and other countries with oppressive regimes. A long
list of other charitable organizations assist the needy, support education,
offer camp scholarships to poor families, deliver weekly food packages to the
destitute, provide stipends to scholars, help underprivileged couples pay for
the weddings, and furnish their homes, etc.

To the outside world the various
Chassidim may appear alike because they seem to dress and to carry themselves
similarly, but there is significant diversity within the Chassidic community.
The varied Chassidic denominations focus on different teachings and on
different leaders. These differences are not only of degree but also touch
matters of interpretation and doctrine. Thus when the first wave of
post-Holocaust immigrants arrived in Montreal, Satmar, Belz, Lubavitch, Tosh
and Skver (the various Chassidic communities that established themselves in
Quebec) established schools for their individual denominations. Non-Chassidic
communities opened their own schools such as Yeshiva Gedlah.

One significant area of difference
between Satmar and various other Chassidic groups concerns the modern State of
Israel. In his treatise
Vayoel Moshe
(1958) and in
Al Hageulah V’al
Hatamurah
(1967), Rabbi Yoel Teitelbaum insisted that the Jewish people
were not to reclaim Israel, or form any sovereign national entity for that
matter, before the coming of the Messiah.

Moreover, he also bristled at the
fact that the founding Zionists were hostile to religion. In his view the
modern State of Israel lacked biblical legitimacy. Others disagreed, arguing
that once the state existed there were practical reasons for supporting its
viability. Rabbi Teitelbaum rejected these arguments, and to this day his view
on the matter prevails in the Satmar community.

It is important to understand that
there is no synod in Judaism that declares religious law. Law is determined by
precedent and the body of hermeneutical interpretation that has shaped this law
over the hundreds of years. There is room within this system of interpretation
for deciders to arrive at differing conclusions as demonstrated by the example
of this issue of the State of Israel.

Conclusion

The Satmar community in Montreal
today consists of roughly 350 families. This modest community is a part of the
world wide Satmar community that undertook to reconstruct the normal patterns
of pre-war communal life after the Holocaust. Led by the Satmar Rabbi and
others who followed in his footsteps they have managed to recreate their
traditions and achieve communal equanimity to a remarkable degree. At the core
of their community stands the congregation, facilitating the transmission of
their values, and their adherence to the moral vision of the Torah. And at the
center of the congregation stands their school system, shaping the new
generations for modern life based on the tenets of their traditional knowledge
and culture. Emerging from a cataclysm perhaps unequalled in history, this
system of faith-steeped schooling has outfitted them to reclaim a culture, a
tradition and a future. From this schooling have emerged citizens who have made
contributions in the many lands where they have settled. At the same time that
they have built schools, charities, and communal institutions, they have
contributed successfully to their local economies, participated as productive
law-abiding citizens and raised steadfast families.
(footnote omitted in part)

[
10
]

On the subject of the Talmudic instruction
provided by the Académie, we reproduce the conclusions of the report by the
expert Bernard Fryshman, Ph.D. (physics), who was born in Montreal and studied
here until 1960. He subsequently moved to New York City, where he is now Professor
of physics at the Faculty of the New York Institute of Technology:

Many outcomes are engendered in
students by Talmudic study which are necessary ingredients in the lifelong
learner. There is a sense of confidence, a willingness to engage in the battles
of the mind, and to challenge which is developed. Students begin to understand
that knowledge must be tested before it is to be accepted. Learning must
involve the person, so that the scholar is more than just intellectually
invested in his topic. The scholar must develop the personal and character
attributes which mark the scholarly personality as well.

Such a system requires a total
immersion, and viewing education as an integral whole, not only enveloping
character and intellect, but also encompassing, in an encyclopedic approach,
all disciplines.  There are no boundaries between subject areas; educated from
childhood in this way, students receive a foundation and perspective which is
invaluable in today’s world.

The overall goals of Talmudic education
are surprisingly congruent with the outcomes aimed at by conventional,
state-sanctioned programs of study. The means, however, differ. The focus is on
developing the intellectual skills, the curiosity, the motivation, and the
confidence for students to continue to learn for the rest of their lives. The
Internet, and its ability to provide facts and information instantly, will
likely encourage others to move in a similar direction.

Such an education does not come
easily. Yeshiva students spend many more hours in study than the norm, and for
many more weeks. Slowly, the program expands to the point where study becomes
an integral part of one’s life.

I have not, for the purposes of
this report and in the limited time period in which is was necessary for me to
produce it, examined in detail the specific program of studies offered by the
Académie Yeshiva Toras Moshe de Montréal and the Quebec Education Program.
However, my experience in matters of accreditation of Talmudic schools allows
me to state without hesitation that it is highly likely that the Yeshiva in
question offers a valid alternative to the conventional program of studies in
the Province of Quebec, and that it produces results that can be said to be
‘equivalent’ to those of the state-sanctioned program of studies.  Almost 60
years of successful teaching and learning should not be discarded. On the
contrary, the Yeshiva Toras Moshe program should be closely examined with a
view to a potential recognition that the Talmudic education that it dispenses,
together with its secular curriculum, offers an acceptable alternative. »

[
11
]

That said, let us now move on to the facts.

III.

THE FACTS

[
12
]

The Satmar Chassidic community has a worldwide
population of about 130,000.

[
13
]

The Montreal community is quite small, consisting
of approximately 350 families living in the Outremont and Mile End
neighbourhoods.

[
14
]

Satmar takes its name from a city located in
Romania (Satu Mare), which was home to the Grand Rabbi Joël Teitelbaum before
the World War II. Just like all of the other Chassidic communities in Eastern
Europe, the Satmar community was devastated during the war. When the war ended,
Rabbi Teitelbaum led the survivors of the community to the Americas. Most
settled in and around New York City, but some also found homes in Los Angeles,
Montreal, and Buenos Aires. The community also has members living in Europe,
Australia, and Israel.

[
15
]

As the expert Kessner notes, the Satmar
community practices an extremely devout form of Judaism, which is based, in
part, on the practice and study of the Talmud. The evidence in this case
reveals that members of the Satmar community consider religious education to be
central to their religious convictions and practices. Presented as a life-long
commitment for the boys and men of the community, it begins around the age of
six and continues for the rest of their lives.

[
16
]

Talmudic teachings are centred on the Torah,
which is the Jewish Bible, and its commentaries, which have been developed over
several generations. These commentaries are generally referred to as the
Talmud. The teaching of the Talmud is an immemorial custom, dating back at
least two thousand years. Talmudic studies constitute not only the means by
which members of the community learn to share their religion but, as the
evidence shows, also a religious obligation with which community members must
comply.

[
17
]

The expert evidence adduced, which at this stage
is uncontradicted, presents the teaching of the Talmud as an integrated whole
which, although religious in nature, leads to a number of intellectual
accomplishments similar to those sought by conventional modern educational
programs.

[
18
]

The Montreal Satmar community founded a Talmudic
school (or Yeshiva) in 1952, which has since operated without interruption.

[
19
]

The Académie was first located on Saint-Urbain
Street in Montreal. In the early 2000s, it became necessary to transfer
operations and for a time it operated out of two sites, a temporary one on
Bates Street and the other on Saint Urbain Street.

[
20
]

The evidence reveals that, since the spring of
2009, all of the Académie's classes have been offered at a new building built
by the defendants on Casgrain Street in Montreal. It should be noted that the
construction of this new building was made possible by donations from members
of the Satmar community, primarily those in Montreal.

[
21
]

Since the foundation of the Académie, the Satmar
community has never requested or received any public funding for its
establishment. Indeed, funding for the Académie has always been ensured
essentially through tuitions and donations. The evidence shows that this choice
was made to preserve the Académie's independence with regard to its ability to
offer religious education complemented by secular, or lay, education in
accordance with the beliefs and practices of the Satmar community.

[
22
]

The Académie now counts 163 students. In
addition to the Talmudic teaching that occupies the greater part of their days,
the young boys attending the Académie also follow so-called secular courses,
essentially classes in English and mathematics, following a program developed
by Jacob Maman who, as we have seen, is the director of secular studies at the
Academie.

[
23
]

The evidence shows that this secular instruction
is limited to approximately six hours a week. Including Talmudic teaching, the
students at the Académie take between twenty-nine hours of class a week their
first year (boys aged six) and forty hours a week in grade six.

[
24
]

The Académie acknowledges that this distribution
of instruction, the subjects taught, and the time devoted to secular subjects
does not correspond to the requirements set out in Quebec legislation. First,
the hours and subjects do not correspond to what is set out in the
Basic
School Regulation
.
[6]

Second, their programs are not consistent with Quebec educational programs,
which are required for all students in Quebec, pursuant to
section 461

E.A.
,
which is applicable to schools subject to the
A.P.E.
under section 32 of
that Act.

[
25
]

On November 2, 2006, following an anonymous tip,
representatives of the Quebec Department of Education, Recreation and Sports
(the "MELS)", specifically Gilles Lamirande, director of the Montreal
Regional Department, and Ugo-Mercier Gouin, professional at the Department's
Private Education Division, visited the Académie's premises on Bates Road in
Montreal. During this visit, which apparently lasted about fifteen minutes,
they observed that elementary educational services were being dispensed to
school-age children.

[
26
]

On November 10, 2006, Lise Briand, director at
the Private Education Division, asked the director of the Académie to inform
her of his intentions regarding the continuation of private instructional
activities and to agree upon a deadline for submission of his application for a
permit.

[
27
]

Ms. Briand stated that the Department considered
that the visit had revealed that the institution was subject to the
Act
respecting Private education
, [
translation
]
"given the nature of the educational services it dispenses". Ms.
Briand added that, this being the case, the Académie was in violation of
section 10 of that Act.

[
28
]

On November 21, 2006, Lamirande and Gouin
allegedly visited facilities, including the one located on Saint-Urban Street,
where they observed that elementary educational services were being dispensed
to school-age students.

[
29
]

On May 30, 2007, the Attorney General sent the
Académie a demand letter on behalf of the Minister, asking that the Académie
and any person connected with it [
translation
]
"cease to operate any educational institution, cease dispensing elementary
and secondary education services and, pursuant to
section 63
of the
Act
respecting Private education
, submit the student's school records and the
register of enrolment, as applicable".
[7]

[
30
]

On June 26, 2007, the Académie requested a
meeting with the Private Education Division of the MELS. In response to this
letter, on July 5, 2007, the Académie was asked first to apply for a permit
pursuant to the

B. Criteria

[15]

[

The tests for granting an interlocutory

752.

Outre l'injonction qu'elle
peut demander par requête introductive d'instance, avec ou sans autres
conclusions, une partie peut, au début ou au cours d'une instance, obtenir
une injonction interlocutoire.

L'injonction
interlocutoire peut être accordée lorsque celui qui la demande paraît y avoir
droit et qu'elle est jugée nécessaire pour empêcher que ne lui soit causé un
préjudice sérieux ou irréparable, ou que ne soit créé un état
de

fait ou
de

droit
de

nature à rendre le jugement final inefficace
.

752
.
In addition to an injunction, which he may demand by a motion to institute
proceedings, with or without other conclusions, a party may, at the
commencement of or during a suit, obtain an interlocutory injunction.

An
interlocutory injunction may be granted when the applicant appears to be
entitled to it and it is considered to be necessary in order to avoid serious
or irreparable injury to him, or a factual or legal situation of such a
nature as to render the final judgment ineffectual.

[
82
]

In
Brassard
,
[16]
LeBel J.A., as he then was,
provided a brilliant synthesis of the tests relevant to ruling on a motion for
interlocutory injunction. It is useful to reproduce lengthy excerpts thereof
here:

[
translation
]

Quebec judicial law, and
particularly that pertaining to injunctions, is not entirely contained in the
Code
of Civil Procedure
(see
Favre v. Hôpital Notre-Dame
,
1984 CanLII 2824 (QC CA)
, [1984] C.A. 548
at 551,
per
Bernier J.A.;
Trudel v. Clairol of
Canada Inc
.,
[1975] S.C.R. 236 at 246, per Pigeon J.). Its provisions, however, and
article
752
C.C.P. in particular, provide the general framework for the consideration
of motions for interlocutory injunctions by Quebec courts and the general
criteria they must take into account. While they may be open to interpretation
or development in the case law, they may not be ignored. Thus, the judge
hearing a motion for interlocutory injunction must consider the
prima facie

right, the irreparable harm, and the weight or balance of convenience for each
of the parties.

...

In 1991, in
Gravel v. Fernand
Gravel Assurance Inc
.,
1991 CanLII 3942 (QC CA)
, [1991] R.D.J. 147 at 148, Monet J.A. reiterated the
tests in
article 752

C.C.P
. The headnotes of that case clearly summarize
the general direction of Quebec case law:

[
translation
]

At
the interlocutory injunction stage, the rights of the applicant are clear,
doubtful, or non-existent, as the case may be. If it appears clear that the
applicant’s rights are founded, then the applicant must demonstrate that he
would suffer serious or irreparable harm. If his right is doubtful, the Court
must weigh the balance of convenience. If it is non-existent, the application
must be dismissed. (See also 152-153, per Monet J.A.)

This opinion highlights two very
important aspects of the implementation of
article 752

C.C.P.
First, it
indicates that there must be a colour of right, the quality of which is likely
to vary. Next, it outlines the relationship between the various tests the
courts must consider. Monet J.A.'s opinion points out, however, that even in a
preliminary or superficial manner, the existence and quality of these remedies
must be verified.
Ultimately, in the absence of a legal basis, fear of even
the most serious harm does not justify issuing an injunction. There is no
remedy without right. Obversely, where there is no evidence of irreparable
harm, even the clearest right does not justify granting an order for
interlocutory injunction. The pointlessness of the remedy would prohibit its
issue
. (Emphasis added.)

Concepts such as "
prima
facie
right" and "colour of right" are not easily defined.
Monet J.A.'s opinion, which, moreover, was based on prior case law to which we
shall return, noted that in this area the judge should not insist on the
demonstration of a firm right. A doubtful or arguable right is an adequate
basis for injunction, provided that irreparable harm is demonstrated and that
the balance of convenience favours the applicant.

In this respect, the so-called
serious question test as set out in a few judgments of the Supreme Court of
Canada (for example, in
J.R. MacDonald v. Attorney General of Canada
,

1994 CanLII 117 (SCC)
, [1994] 1 S.C.R. 311 at 335 and 335,
per
Cory and Sopinka JJ.;
Manitoba
(Attorney General) v
.
Metropolitan Stores Ltd.
,
1987 CanLII 79 (SCC)
, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 110
at 128; see also
Attorney General of Quebec v. Poirier
,
J.E. 95-820
(6
April, 1995) (C.A.)), does not appear to require a process distinct from that
used to determine a colour of right. Quebec judicial law recognizes that even a
doubtful right determined upon a cursory, preliminary analysis of the legal and
factual foundations of the case may serve as the basis for a motion for
injunction. The "serious question test" does not dispense with the
need for a thoughtful consideration of the strength of the legal arguments, to
the extent that it actually differs from the test for a serious colour of
right.

...

A few years later, in S
ociété de
développement de la Baie-James et al. v. Kanatewat et a
l.,
[1975] C.A. 167
,
this Court once again applied the tests in
article 752

C.C.P.
Among the
many complex questions before the Court in that case was the nature of the
colour of right and of the interrelationship between the factors that courts
must consider before issuing an interlocutory injunction order. Owen J.A.'s
opinion considered these issues specifically, providing a framework for
analysis that has subsequently been applied in other judgments. In the view of
Owen J.A., the applicant must demonstrate first a right and then an irreparable
harm. If the right is doubtful, particular attention should also be given to
weighing the balance of convenience:

Article
752 C.P. provides that the applicant for an interlocutory injunction must pass
two tests or surmount two successive obstacles.

First
the applicant has to convince the Court that he appears to be entitled to an
interlocutory injunction, that is that the right he is asserting has a
reasonable prospect of being recognized by the final judgment. Secondly the
applicant, if successful on the first test, then has to show that it is an
exceptional case in which an interlocutory injunction is necessary in order to
avoid: (i) serious or irreparable injury to the applicant, or (ii) a factual or
legal situation of such a nature as to render the final judgment ineffectual
.

The
present Respondents claim that they have certain rights in the territory and
that in virtue of these rights they are entitled to an interlocutory injunction
against the present Appellants.

At
the interlocutory injunction stage these rights are apparently either (a)
clear, or (b) doubtful, or (c) non-existent.

(a)
If it appears clear, at the interlocutory stage that the Petitioners have the
rights which they invoke then the interlocutory injunction should be granted if
considered necessary in accordance with the provisions of the second paragraph
of Article 752 C.P.

(b)
However, if at this stage the existence of the rights invoked by the
Petitioners appears doubtful then the Court should consider the balance of
convenience and inconvenience in deciding whether an interlocutory injunction
should be granted.

(c)
Finally if it appears at the interlocutory stage, that the rights claimed are
non-existent then the interlocutory injunction should be refused.

(See
opinion of Owen J. at 183- 184;
see also
Favre v. Hôpital Notre-Dame
,
per

Bernier J. at 550-551 and
Coutu v. L'Ordre des Pharmaciens
(12
January 1992) Montreal 09-000683-797 (C.A.) at 13 and 17, Jacques J.A.)

What is more, in
Coutu
,
Jacques J.A. highlights the importance of considering the quality of the colour
of right and its relationship with the other tests to be considered. The weaker
the colour of right, the greater the need for attentiveness when considering
the irreparability of the injury and, if necessary, the balance of convenience.

[
translation
]

In
this case, if the Order's right is clear and certain, the slightest harm or
serious possibility of harm to the rights of the public or to public order may
be sufficient to render the injunction necessary; if its right is doubtful, the
purported injury must be greater than that of the appellants. (Opinion of
Jacques J.A. at 17).

The consideration of colour of
right requires prudence. The judge is not hearing the merits of the
application; rather, he or she must assess the merits of the grounds raised
only to be satisfied of the existence and quality of the colour of right. As
soon as the grounds appear sufficiently serious to present a reasonable chance
of success, the judge must find that the applicant has satisfied the first
requirement in
article 752

C.C.P
. Indeed, this was noted by McCarthy
J.A.:

[
translation
]

Concerning
the motion for interlocutory injunction itself, it is important to note at the
outset that neither the Superior Court nor this Court is being asked to decide
the right. The issue in such a motion is not the right, but the colour of
right.... (see
Simon v. Municipality of Oka
,
1991 CanLII 3175 (QC CA)
,
[1992] R.D.J.

148 at 152,
per
McCarthy J.A. (C.A.);
see also
Favre v. Hôpital Notre-Dame
,
per
Bernier
J. at 552;
Royal Bank of Canada v. Propriété Cité Concordia
,
1983 CanLII 2764 (QC CA)
,
[1983]
R.D.J. 524
at 527,
per
Montgomery J.A. (C.A.).

The nature of
article 752

C.C.P
. and its interpretation in the case law
impose on this Court a duty to verify whether there is a colour of right or
serious questions of law to be tried that justify finding that such issues
exist.
They do not authorize making a decision on the merits of the case,
save indirectly, to the extent that it may be concluded that a fundamental
weakness of the remedy deprives it of a legal basis.
(Emphasis added.)

[
83
]

LeBel J.A, as he then was, applying these
principles to the case before him, found that there was no colour of right, set
aside the judgment of the Superior Court, and dismissed the motion for
interlocutory injunction.

[
84
]

An example illustrating this last comment of
LeBel J.A., as he then was, is
Tremblay v. Daigle
,
[17]
where the Supreme Court dismissed
a motion for interlocutory injunction because of a lack of legal basis.

[
85
]

The Attorney General emphasizes that the Court
must not rule on the merits, as indeed LeBel J.A.. stated in Brasard. It is
worth observing, however, that orders sought at the interlocutory stage and at
the permanent stage are similar.

[
86
]

Whatever the case may be, these reasons should
not be seen in any way as prejudging the subsequent decision on the merits.

[
87
]

It is now time to determine whether, in light of
these principles, the applicant meets the tests for issuing the orders for
interlocutory injunction sought.

1.
Serious colour of right

[
88
]

The Attorney General argues that this case
presents a serious colour of right. Let us consider.

[
89
]

Section 10
of the
A.P.E.
is the legal
basis of the interlocutory injunction sought in this case. This provision reads
as follows:

10.
Nul ne
peut tenir un établissement d'enseignement
privé
auquel
s'applique la présente
loi
, s'il n'est titulaire d'un permis délivré par
le ministre pour l'établissement et les services éducatifs ou catégories de

10.

[
90
]

There is no doubt in this case that the Académie
"operates a private educational institution";
section 3
of the
A.P.E
.
creates an irrebutable presumption of this fact, as the Académie dispenses
educational services, primarily Talmudic education, for non-profit purposes.

[
91
]

A final and decisive question remains, however:
Does the Académie operate a private educational institution "to which this
Act applies"?

[
92
]

Whether or not the Académie is private is not at
issue.

[
93
]

As for the term "...to which this Act
applies",
section 1
of the
A.P.E.

provides that the Act applies to
every private educational institution dispensing all or some of the educational

[
94
]

It now remains to be determined whether the
Académie dispenses elementary school instructional services.

[
95
]

Section 2

A.P.E.
stipulates that
paragraph 2 of section 1 of this Act refers to "education or instruction
intended mainly to develop students' abilities in subjects preparing them for

level, as the case may be".

[
96
]

The evidence reveals that education and
instruction dispensed by the Académie are in no way intended to develop
students' abilities in subjects preparing them for studies at the elementary,
secondary, postsecondary, college or university level, as the case may be.

[
97
]

The educational services dispensed by the
Académie are primarily intended to prepare the students for more advanced

mainly in New York. The record shows that it is actually a
[translation]
"religious
school" and has always been considered as such by the members of the
community.

[
98
]

As for the secular English and math classes that
constitute a portion of the curriculum, they are intended to enable the
students to function effectively in society. In no way do they seek to prepare
students for studies at the secondary, postsecondary, college or university
level. The evidence shows that this secular aspect of the instruction is a sort
of "survival tool" for the students.

[
99
]

Paragraphs 2 and 3 of section 2 of the
School
Regulation
[18]

appear to confirm the legislative intent to limit the application of the
A.P.E.

to educational institutions that are part of the elementary, secondary,
postsecondary, college and university continuum. These provisions read as
follows:

Les services d'enseignement
primaire

ont pour but
de
permettre le développement intégral
de

l'élève et son insertion dans la société par des apprentissages fondamentaux
qui contribueront au développement progressif
de
son
autonomie et qui lui permettront d'accéder aux savoirs proposés à
l'enseignement

secondaire.

ont pour but
de
poursuivre le développement intégral
de

l'élève,

de
base
de

[
100
]

Moreover, according to the arguments of counsel
for the parties, institutions offering tutoring (in French, English, and math,
for example) are not considered by the MELS to be subject to the obligation to
hold a permit under the
A.P.E.

[
101
]

The Attorney General, for his part, argues that
the current situation infringes the rights and obligations of the children with
regard to compulsory attendance at school and their right to the educational
services outlined the
School Regulation
. With respect, this is a
separate issue, to which the Court will later return.

[
102
]

The second element of
section 10
of the
A.P.E
.
stipulates: "...unless he is the holder of a permit, issued by the
Minister, for the institution and the educational services or categories of
educational services mentioned in
section 1
that are dispensed". The
Attorney General argues that, by not holding a permit issued by the Minister,
the Académie infringes section 10 of the Act.

[
103
]

The Académie, for its part, admits that it does
not hold a permit issued by the Minister for its institution but argues that
such a permit is not required because it does not operate an educational
institution to which the
A.P.E
. applies.

[
104
]

Regarding the permit, the Académie states that,
if it is in fact required to hold such a permit, the Minister's refusal to
issue it is unjustified in this case. It also argues that the Minister should
have granted its application for an exemption under
paragraph 2
of
section 22

of the
Regulation
.

[
105
]

At this stage of proceedings, these questions
relating to the permit or the application for exemption need not be answered.
It is sufficient to note that the Académie does not hold a permit issued by the
Minister.

[
106
]

Given that the Supreme Court of Canada has not
been particularly demanding with regard to this first test,
[19]
the Court finds that the Attorney
General has established a colour of right.

[
107
]

Based on the foregoing, however, this colour of
right is doubtful. This is important, given the interrelationship of the three
tests that must be met for the interlocutory injunction sought in this case to
be granted.

2.
Irreparable harm

[
108
]

According to the Attorney General, the very
failure to comply with a public order statute constitutes irreparable harm.
Therefore, he argues, the operation of a private educational institution
without a permit is clearly unlawful and causes irreparable harm that compels
the granting of an interlocutory injunction.

[
109
]

The Académie replies that it is not subject to
the
A.P.E.
and that it therefore is not in violation of it. As a result,
the claim that the provisions of that Act are being continuously violated
during the trial and until the final adjudication on the merits is false.

[
110
]

The Court must determine whether the refusal to
grant the interlocutory injunction sought would in this case cause irreparable
harm or create a factual or legal situation that would render the final
judgment ineffective.

[
111
]

It is important to point out at the outset that
the interlocutory injunction is granted only to
avoid
irreparable harm
and not to issue a remedy for the applicant during the proceedings. The wording
of paragraph 2 of
article 752

C.C.P
. is unequivocal in this respect.

[
112
]

In this case, it is argued that the
A.P.E
.,
which the Attorney General characterizes as a public interest and public order
statute, is being violated during the proceedings.

[
113
]

In principle, a litigant who does not challenge
the constitutional validity of such an act should not object to complying with
it during the proceedings. Indeed, public interest lies in the presumption of
the validity of statutes.

[
114
]

This case, however, raises rather delicate
questions in circumstances which may be described as exceptional.

[
115
]

The Court has already found that the colour of
right in this case is doubtful. The weaker the colour of right, the greater the
irreparable harm must be.

[
116
]

The Attorney General invokes the protection of
the public interest. It should be pointed out, however, that the Académie has
been operating as an educational institution since 1952 without any action
being brought against it and without being found guilty of anything whatsoever.
The
A.P.E
. came into force in July of 1993, and there have been no
lawsuits or judgments against it since then.
[20]

Later, we shall discuss the statute that preceded the
A.P.E
.

[
117
]

The Académie raises serious arguments, in
particular the unjustified refusal of a permit and the rejection of the
application for exemption pursuant to
paragraph 2
of
section 22
of the
Regulation
,

which authorizes the Minister to exempt a religious non-profit organization
from the compulsory
subjects
to be taught,
programs
to be
followed, and
textbooks
to be used. Finally, it argues that its freedom
of religion would be infringed were it obliged to comply with the
School Regulation.

[
118
]

After weighing all the factors, the Court is not
convinced that the Attorney General has demonstrated that the refusal to grant
the interlocutory injunction would cause irreparable harm.

[
119
]

The Court is of the view, however, that the
motion for injunction may be considered necessary to avoid the creation of a
factual or legal situation rendering the final judgment ineffective in this
case, specifically with respect to the 163 children who attend the Académie.

[
120
]

Indeed, a final judgment in favour of the
Attorney General could not retroactively remedy the lack of obligatory
educational services the children should have received.

[
121
]

It is true that the children and their parents
have no complaints regarding the educational services dispensed by the Académie.
On the other hand, the State has a certain – indeed, a definite – interest in
the education and instruction of its citizens. The interests of the parties
must therefore be weighed against each other. To do so, we must determine on
whom the obligation to attend school is incumbent and which means the State has
chosen to ensure compliance with that obligation. The Court shall consider
these issues at length below.

3.
Balance of convenience

[
122
]

The Attorney General states that the balance of
convenience weighs in its favour in matters concerning the consistent
application of a public interest statute. Moreover, it argues that a
comparative assessment of the balance of convenience must also weigh in its
favour.

[
123
]

In its view, it is not impossible for the
Académie to comply with the Act during the proceedings. The fact that the the
young boys registered at the Académie would attend another school or be
home-schooled for the duration of the proceedings does not outweigh the
inconvenience that would be caused the Attorney General.

[
124
]

The defendants, for their part, argue that the
children, their parents, and their families would suffer serious harm if the
interlocutory injunction were issued and that, consequently, the balance of
convenience clearly weighs in their favour.

[
125
]

The sudden interruption in the children's
secular English and mathematics classes, which are their survival tools for
society since most of their instruction is primarily religious and received in
Aramaic, ancient Hebrew, and Yiddish, would cause them serious harm.

[
126
]

The evidence reveals that placing the children
in other educational institutions would be impossible on religious grounds,
given the Satmar community's strict religious practices.

[
127
]

It is interesting – indeed, even astonishing –
that it is only at this stage that the parties bother with the best interest of
the 163 children affected in this case, even though the law requires everyone,
including the Court, to make any decision in light of their interests and the
respect of their rights: article 33
C.C.Q
.

[
128
]

None of the children were called, heard, or
represented in this case. Only one parent, Abraham Ekstein, intervened,
although the defendant administrators are for the most part parents as well.

[
129
]

The evidence is clearly insufficient for the
Court to determine which of the following is in the best interests of the
children involved in this case:

- the compulsory curriculum

established through Quebec
legislation; or

- the educational services dispensed at the Académie in the respect
of their freedom of religion, based on their sincere beliefs.

[
130
]

This question being asked, it should be recalled
that the balance of convenience must be weighed, since the Court has determined
that the Attorney General's colour of right was doubtful. Such uncertainty,
however, cannot be used to tip the scales in favour of the defendants.

[
131
]

On the one hand, public interest favours the
Attorney General; on the other, fundamental
Charter

rights favour the defendants.

[
132
]

Case law teaches that public interest must take
priority over the interests of private litigants.
[21]

[
133
]

It must therefore be concluded that the balance
of convenience favours the Attorney General.

4.

The
discretionary power of the Court

[
134
]

It should be pointed out that the Court is
being asked to decide a motion for interlocutory injunction. Although the rules
governing such a remedy are partially codified in the
Code of Civil
Procedure
, this remedy finds its origins in the common law.
[22]

[
135
]

A motion for interlocutory injunction, as its
name suggests, seeks to obtain an order from the Superior Court for the
duration of proceedings. Thus, it is an order of the Court issued before the
parties have had the opportunity to be heard in a full trial. Indeed, to date,
the trial remains to date the means by which the rights of the parties involved
are determined.

[
136
]

Some circumstances, however, require that
certain orders be made to prevent one of the parties from suffering irreparable
injury before the trial is held. As a result, over the centuries, courts have
developed rules enabling them to render partial justice to the parties before
the trial.

[
137
]

That is why, in this judgment, the Court has set
out and applied the three main tests that have been developed to enable it to
rule on the motion for interlocutory injunction sought in this case.

[
138
]

However, given the delicate position of the
Court and the essential incompleteness of the record on which it must rule,
among other things, the courts have always emphasized the essentially
discretionary nature of the injunctive remedy.

[
139
]

The Quebec legislature has characterized this
remedy as a "special proceeding" or even a “provisional remedy”.
Scholarly commentary also describes it as [
translation
]
"an exclusive and exceptional remedy".
[23]
Fundamentally, however, an
injunction is discretionary: the Court that must rule on such an action enjoys
broad discretionary powers.
[24]

The Supreme Court of Canada has confirmed as much on several occasions.
[25]

[
140
]

The Court’s discretion must nevertheless be
exercised both judicially and judiciously. It is worth citing the dictum of
Lord Halsbury in
Sharp v. Wakefield:
[26]

It is to be, not arbitrary, vague
and fanciful, but legal and regular. And it must be exercised within the limit,
to which an honest man, competent to the discharge of his office ought to
confine himself.

[
141
]

After having analyzed the record as a whole and
after considered reflection, the Court finds that, in this case, it must
exercise its discretionary power to refuse the motion for interlocutory
injunction sought by the Attorney General

[
142
]

Indeed, the Court finds that a trial must be
held in order to make an informed decision with regard to the numerous
difficult and delicate issues and their complex ramifications that this case
raises.

[
143
]

The following five reasons lead the Court to
exercise its discretionary power in this way:

(a) the time that has passed since 1952;

(b) the right of the children involved;

(c) the existence of another remedy;

(d) the attempt to judicialize the children's compulsory school
attendance; and

(e) the lack of usefulness, effectiveness, and enforceability of the
injunction.

[
144
]

I shall now provide brief explanations for each
of these reasons:

(a) the time
that has passed since 1952

[
145
]

The Académie has been providing educational
services to boys in the Chasidic community since 1952. The Attorney General's
motion for interlocutory and permanent injunction was not filed until April 22,
2010.

[
146
]

Even if we do not take into account the time passed
between November 2006 and April 2010 – as the parties have agreed – the period
of time between 1952 and October 2006 remains an obstacle that cannot be
ignored in the circumstances and justifies the exercise of the Court's
discretion in this case.

[
147
]

First, although the legislature does not dictate
that urgency is a necessary prerequisite to the granting of an interlocutory
injunction as it is for a provisional injunction, case law has often found that
a long period of time constitutes a significant obstacle to issuing an
interlocutory injunction.
[27]

Second, this period of time is inconsistent with the notion of urgency that
usually underlies the need for an interlocutory order to prevent irreparable
harm to one of the parties.
[28]

[
148
]

It should be recalled that the
A.P.E
., on
which the motion for injunction is based, came into force on July 1, 1993.
[29]
Before that, the
Private
Education Act
,
[30]

which came into force on December 18, 1968, contained a provision (section
23) similar to
section 10
of the
A.P.E
., on which the motion for
interlocutory injunction is based.

[
149
]

Nevertheless, since 1968, the Académie has been
subjected to no injunction, charge, or conviction judgment against it for
having operated an educational institution without holding a valid permit
issued by the Minister for this purpose.

(b) the right of
the children involved

[
150
]

The parties admit that this dispute directly
concerns 163 children of the Satmar Chassidic community. Neither these children
nor their parents were called, represented, or heard.

[
151
]

Moreover, the record is clearly incomplete.
Consequently, the Court is unable to make a fair ruling on a motion that will
necessarily affect the civil and constitutional rights of these persons.

[
152
]

While the documentation submitted to the Court
is particularly voluminous, the fact remains that the evidence adduced in this
case is clearly insufficient to justify a ruling – even a preliminary one – on
the rights of the children concerned.

[
153
]

Indeed, at this stage, the Court is ill-equipped
to determine the necessity of the compulsory curriculum enacted by the State.

[
154
]

Moreover, the Supreme Court of Canada is
currently deliberating on
S. L. v. Commission scolaire des Chênes
,
[31]
which was heard
en banc
on
May 18 of this year. In that case, the Supreme Court must rule on the validity
of the refusal of an application for exemption from the Ethics and Religious
Culture courses made by the parents of a minor child, based on their sincere
religious beliefs. This application for exception was made pursuant to

paragraph 2
of
section 222
of the
E
.
A.
,
[32]
which is
identical to that in
paragraph 1
of
section 30
of the
A.P.E.
.

[
155
]

Thus, the judgment the Supreme Court will render
shortly in
S .L.
will likely have an impact on one or more aspects of
the case before us. Justice therefore requires the Court to wait for guidance
from the highest court in the land.

(c) the
existence of another remedy

[
156
]

Case law has recognized that the Court may, in
the exercise of its discretion, consider whether there is another appropriate
remedy available to the plaintiff.

[
157
]

Here, the
A.P.E.

sets out administrative
sanctions in Chapter IX and penal sanctions in Chapter X. Section 128 in
Chapter X sets out a penalty in the case of a violation of section 10 of the
Act. Section 136 states that the fines are doubled in the case of a second
offence. These provisions state:

128.

Quiconque contrevient à l'une des dispositions des
articles 10, 11 ou 55 est passible d'une amende de 500 $ à
5 000 $, dans le cas d'une personne physique ou, dans le cas d'une
personne morale, d'une amende de 1 000 $ à 10 000 $.

136.

En cas de récidive, les amendes prévues pour l'infraction en cause sont
portées au double
.

128.

Every person who contravenes any of the provisions of sections 10, 11 and 55
is liable to a fine of $500 to $5,000 in the case of a natural person, or, in
the case of a legal person, to a fine of $1,000 to $10,000.

136.

In the case of a second offence, the fines prescribed for the offence
concerned shall be doubled
.

[
158
]

These penalties contrast sharply with those
available in the case of infringement of an order of injunction, namely, a fine
not exceeding $50,000, with or without imprisonment for a period of up to one
year, without prejudice to the right to recover damages (
article 761

C.C.P.
).

[
159
]

In
Pharmascience
,
[33]
LeBel J., for the majority,
states that the existence of a specific sanction defined in a particular
statute does not necessarily preclude the issuing of an order for injunction
based on the general law when circumstances so require. Nevertheless, the existence
of another remedy constitutes one of the circumstances the Court must weigh
when exercising its discretionary power and deciding whether it would be
justified in granting the injunction sought.

[
160
]

Pharmascience
should,
however, be distinguished from the present case. In that case, evidence of
multiple court challenges and the trouble the trustee Binet had in obtaining
the documents required for his investigation made it possible for Déziel J.,
exercising his discretion, to find that Pharmascience's refusal and its
behaviour was intended to paralyze the trustee Binet's investigation and that
it therefore justified the granting of an injunction.

[
161
]

City of Montreal v
.
Morgan
[34]

should also be distinguished from the case before us. In that case, the
party refused to comply with a municipal by-law and simply paid the penalty set
out in the regulation repeatedly. The Supreme Court found that the right to
infringe a law or by-law cannot be bought by paying a penalty and that, in such
a case, the Court may issue an injunction to prevent further infringement of
the law or by-law. It is worth noting, however, that there was another
statutory provision in that case, namely, article 1066 of the
Civil Code of
Lower Canada
, that justified granting the order of injunction sought by the
City of Montreal and that set out no penal sanctions to ensure compliance.

[
162
]

In the present case, there is no legal provision
other than
section 10

A.P.E.

to justify making an order of injunction,
and this provision prevents only the operation of a private educational
institution. Indeed, the Quebec legislature specifically enacted
sections 128

and
136

A.P.E
. to ensure compliance with section 10 of the
A.P.E
.

[
163
]

Moreover, there is no evidence that these penal
provisions are an ineffective statutory remedy, that the Académie repeatedly
infringed the law, or that it does not intend to comply with it. On the
contrary, one fact in this case is indisputable: in more than half a century,
no penal complaint has ever been brought against the Académie. And there is
more.

[
164
]

A consideration of Quebec legislation as a whole
leads the Court to find that the Quebec legislature has on several occasions
found it appropriate to expressly uphold the right to injunction to ensure
compliance with and the application of a statute that contains penal
provisions. Section 122, in the "Penal Provisions" chapter of the
Pesticides
Act
,
[35]

is but one example among many. It reads as follows:

122.

Aucun recours devant
les
tribunaux civils
n'est suspendu du fait qu'il met en cause un acte ou une omission constituant
une infraction au sens de la présente
loi
.

122.

No civil proceedings shall be suspended on the ground that they pertain to an
act or an omission that constitutes an offence under this Act.

[
165
]

Moreover, it is interesting to note that the
Quebec legislature found it necessary to enact a general provision making
available an injunction against any persons who operate an establishment
without holding the required permit, despite the penal remedies specifically
set out in the various tax statutes. The wording of this provision merits
further consideration, as it allows the issuance of an injunction not only to
order the closing of the establishment but also the cessation of an activity.

of the
Tax Administration Act

[36]
reads as
follows:

En plus des recours spécialement prévus pour toute
violation d'une
loi

fiscale
,
le ministre peut demander à un juge de la Cour supérieure de prononcer contre

procédure civile (chapitre C-25

s'appliquent pas à une demande d'injonction prévue par le présent article.
