the
Code of Civil Procedure
(chapter C-25) applicable to motions made
during proceedings, with the necessary modifications.

The
judge before whom the application for an injunction is presented may make any
other order that he considers necessary to carry out the order of injunction.

Proof
that the person against whom an injunction is applied for keeps an
establishment or carries on an activity for which a certificate, permit or
registration number is required, without holding such a certificate or permit
still in force or without being duly registered, constitutes sufficient proof
to grant the injunction.

The
provisions on injunctions in the
Code of Civil Procedure
do not apply to an
application for an injunction under this section.

[
166
]

As the Court pointed out earlier, the motion for
injunction originates in the common law. It can therefore be useful to
ascertain how the legislatures of other provinces, where the common law is
applied, have maintained the right to injunction to ensure compliance with a
statute that contains penal provisions. For example, the
Independent School
Act
[37]

is equivalent to the
A.P.E.
Section 19(3) of that statute
corresponds to
section 10

A.P.E
., and
section 19(5)
corresponds to
section 128 of the
A.P.E.
and creates an offence when a person infringes
section 19(3) of that Act. The legislature of British Columbia has expressly
maintained the right to interlocutory injunction in addition to the penal
provisions.
[38]

[
167
]

If it is true that the legislature does not
speak gratuitously, then
a fortiori
, it also does not remain silent
without reason.

[
168
]

Consequently, given the clearly expressed intent
of the Quebec legislature in section 128
A.P.E
. and the lack of evidence
that this penal remedy is ineffective in this case, the Court finds that motion
for interlocutory injunction is premature.

(d) the attempt to judicialize the children's compulsory school
attendance

[
169
]

The Court is of the view that, by bringing a
motion for interlocutory injunction, the Attorney General is attempting to
judicialize the compulsory school attendance of children between the ages of
six and sixteen residing in Quebec. On July 1, 1989, the Quebec legislature
chose to dejudicialize compulsory school attendance by enacting
sections 14
to

18
of the

E
.A.
[39]

The wording of these sections and the relevant legislative debates confirm the
legislative intent.
[40]

[
170
]

The dejudicialization of compulsory school
attendance for children between the ages of six and sixteen followed upon the
judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada in
R. v. Jones
.
[41]
In that case, the Court upheld
the conviction of a pastor who refused to send his three children to public
school on religious grounds. The Court found that the legal provisions dealing
with compulsory school attendance for children were constitutionally valid. La
Forest J., however, writing for himself, Dickson C.J. and Lamer J., stated the
following, at para. 25:

How far the province could go in imposing conditions on the way the
appellant provides instruction, if he had applied for registration of his
academy as a private school or for certification of the efficiency of his
instruction, I need not enter into. Certainly a reasonable accommodation
would have to be made in dealing with this issue to ensure that provincial
interests in the quality of education were met in a way that did not unduly
encroach on the religious convictions of the appellant.
In determining
whether pupils are under "efficient instruction", it would be
necessary to delicately and sensitively weigh the competing interests so as
to respect, as much as possible, the religious convictions of the appellant
as guaranteed by the
Charter
. Those who administer the province's
educational requirements may not do so in a manner that unreasonably
infringes on the right of parents to teach their children in accordance with
their religious convictions. The interference must be demonstrably justified.

(Emphasis added.)

Il ne m'est pas nécessaire d'examiner jusqu'à
quel point la province pourrait imposer des conditions sur la manière dont
l'appelant peut assurer l'enseignement, s'il avait demandé l'enregistrement
de son école à titre d'école privée ou l'attestation du caractère approprié
de son enseignement. Il faudrait certainement en arriver à un compromis
raisonnable en examinant cette question afin d'assurer que soient respectés
les intérêts qu'a la province dans la qualité de l'enseignement d'une manière
qui n'empiète pas indûment sur les convictions religieuses de l'appelant.
Pour
déterminer si les élèves reçoivent un "enseignement approprié", il
serait nécessaire d'évaluer avec délicatesse et tact les intérêts opposés, de
manière à respecter, autant que possible, les convictions religieuses de
l'appelant que protège la
Charte
. Ceux qui appliquent la
réglementation de la province en matière d'éducation ne doivent pas le faire
d'une manière qui empiète de façon déraisonnable sur le droit des parents de
donner à leurs enfants un enseignement conforme à leurs convictions religieuses.
La justification de l'atteinte doit pouvoir se démontrer

[
171
]

The number of different opinions expressed in
Jones

demonstrates the complexity of the relationship between the State's
interest in the education of its citizens, the right of parents to see to the
education of their children, and the best interests of these children, while
respecting  fundamental freedoms, within the limits of a free and democratic
society. Clearly, the solution to this problem represents a sizable challenge
to the judiciary.

[
172
]

It is worth pointing out that the parliamentary
debates
[42]

leading up to the enactment of the
A.P.E
. on July 1, 1993, and the
subsequent enactment of
section 22
of the
Regulation
testify to the concern
of the legislature with creating a safety valve whereby the
A.P.E
. would
be constitutionally valid, in accordance with the teachings in
Jones
.

[
173
]

Indeed, a duty of accommodation may also arise
from the freedom of religion guaranteed by the Canadian and Quebec
Charters
.
[43]
Indeed, section 22 of the
Regulation

was enacted to permit such accommodation where needed.

[
174
]

We should recall that the refusal of the
application for exemption based on
paragraph 2
of
section 22
of the
Regulation

is contested by the Académie.

[
175
]

As for compulsory school attendance, it is
required for children, while parents must take the necessary measures to ensure
their children fulfil their obligation to attend school (
sections 14
and
17

E.A
.).
[44]

[
176
]

Section 18
of the
E.A.
establishes the
mechanism whereby the statute ensures that children comply with their
compulsory obligation to attend school. This provision reads as follows:

18
.
Le directeur de l'école s'assure, selon les modalités
établies par la commission scolaire, que les élèves fréquentent assidûment
l'école.

En cas d'absences répétées
et non motivées d'un élève, le directeur de l'école ou la personne qu'il
désigne intervient auprès de l'élève et de ses parents en vue d'en venir à
une entente avec eux et avec les personnes qui dispensent les services
sociaux scolaires sur les mesures les plus appropriées pour remédier à la
situation.

Lorsque l'intervention n'a
pas permis de remédier à la situation, le directeur de l'école le signale au
directeur de la protection de la jeunesse après en avoir avisé par écrit les
parents de l'élève.

18.

The principal shall ascertain, in the manner determined by the
school board, that students attend school regularly.

Where a
student is repeatedly absent without a valid excuse, the principal or the
person designated by him shall intervene with the student and his parents to
come to an agreement with them and with the persons providing the school social
services with respect to the most appropriate measures to remedy the
situation.

When the
intervention does not allow the situation to be remedied, the principal,
after notifying the parents of the student in writing, shall report it to the
director of youth protection.
»

[
177
]

The
Youth Protection Act
[45]
governs the
work of the Director of Youth Protection and contains various provisions aiming
to ensure that children fulfill their obligation of compulsory school
attendance. Moreover, subsection 91(
k
) provides that the tribunal may
order that a child attend a school or another place of learning or participate
in a program geared to developing skills and autonomy. The term
"tribunal", defined in section 1(
g
) of this Act, refers to the
Court of Quebec. As part of the dejudicialization process, the legislature has
imposed the duty to ensure compliance with the obligation to attend school on a
specialized tribunal, where children and parents are called to testify
individually.

[
178
]

Consequently, in light of all of these
legislative provisions, it is difficult to understand how the obligation to
attend school may be sanctioned by the Court by means of an interlocutory injunction
against a private educational institution that does not hold a permit pursuant
to the
A.P.E
.

(e) the lack of usefulness, effectiveness, and enforceability of the
injunction.

[
179
]

As LeBel J.A., as he then was, noted in
Brassard
,

supra
, the notion of usefulness is clearly relevant in matters
concerning interlocutory injunctions.

[
180
]

The Court has attempted to understand the logic
of the Attorney General, who is unhappy with the fact that, in this case, the
children receive only six hours of secular instruction a week, whereas the
School
Regulation
stipulates that they should be receiving twenty-five.

[
181
]

But the Court’s attempts have been in vain.

[
182
]

The order of injunction sought by the Attorney
General seeks to prevent the Académie from providing those six hours of secular
instruction.

[
183
]

There is nothing to indicate that an
interlocutory injunction would be effective in this case, that is, that it
would promote the public interest, which necessarily takes into account the
best interests of the children concerned. In short, it is unlikely that the
remedy sought would be effective (
article 462

C.C.P
.).

[
184
]

Finally, an order of injunction, like any
judgment, must be enforceable within the meaning of
article 469

C.C.P
.
An attentive consideration of all of the statutory provisions, however, leads
the Court to doubt that compliance with these provisions can be ensured by
means of orders for interlocutory injunction in this case.

[
185
]

In Canada’s free and democratic society, parties
are free to act as they wish, subject to prohibitive and public order statutes.
As for the Court, its role is to interpret and apply the law, not to
legislate.

[
186
]

The Court has combed Quebec legislature in vain
for a provision similar to the definition of "private school" in

section 1(1)
of
Ontario's
Education Act.
[46]
This expression is defined thus
by the Ontario legislature

1(1). ...
« École
privée » Établissement qui, entre 9h et 16h un jour de classe, dispense
à cinq élèves ou plus qui ont atteint ou dépassé l’âge de scolarité
obligatoire un enseignement portant sur toute matière du programme d’études
du niveau élémentaire ou secondaire et qui n’est pas une école au sens du
présent article.

1
.(1) ...
“private school” means an institution at which
instruction is provided at any time between the hours of 9 a.m. and 4 p.m. on
any school day for five or more pupils who are of or over compulsory school
age in any of the subjects of the elementary or secondary school courses of
study and that is not a school as defined in this section.

[
187
]

At first sight, this gap in the Quebec
legislation seems to influence the enforceability of the injunction sought,
given the weighty sanctions set out in
article 761

C.C.P
.

[
188
]

Therefore, because of a lack of usefulness,
effectiveness, and enforceability, the Court is of the view that it is
appropriate in the circumstances to exercise its discretionary power and refuse
to grant the orders of interlocutory injunction sought by the Attorney General.

VIII
.      CONCLUSION

[
189
]

This case raises important and sensitive issues,
both legal and social, particularly since, at the heart of it, lies the
question of the education of more than a hundred and fifty children. We must
therefore be all the more prudent in coming to a decision. Clearly, circumstances
require that a full trial be held, to ensure that all of the parties concerned
may be duly represented and heard in full. Such a rigorous judicial process is
a precondition to a considered and enlightened decision, which may only be made
once all of the consequences on every party affected by the dispute have been
weighed.

[
190
]

In the circumstances, in this sensitive
situation with complex ramifications, a hasty judgment must be avoided.

[
191
]

In
Wisconsin v. Yoder
, a decision of the
Supreme Court of the United States, Burger C.J., for the majority,
[47]
wrote that the parents, members
of the Amish community, were justified in withdrawing their fourteen- and
fifteen-year-old children from public school despite compulsory school
attendance until the age of sixteen. That judgment, rendered by the highest
court of the United States, although in a different constitutional context and
nearly forty years ago, is still relevant to us today, particularly where
Burger C.J. states:

We must not forget that, in the
Middle Ages, important values of the civilization of the Western World were
preserved by members of religious orders who isolated themselves from all
worldly influences against great obstacles. There can be no assumption that
today’s majority is "right," and the Amish and others like them are
"wrong."  A way of life that is odd or even erratic but interferes
with no rights or interests of others is not to be condemned because it is
different.
[48]

[
192
]

Closer to home, a highly respected Canadian
jurist for whom compassion constituted a fundamental value, Dickson J., as he
then was, stated the following in
Big M Drug Mart
:
[49]

What
may appear good and true to a majoritarian religious group, or to the state
acting at their behest, may not, for religious reasons, be imposed upon
citizens who take a contrary view. The
Charter
safeguards religious
minorities from the threat of "the tyranny of the majority.
"

Une
majorité religieuse, ou l'état à sa demande ne peut, pour des motifs
religieux, imposer sa propre conception de ce qui est bon et vrai aux
citoyens qui ne partagent pas le même point de vue. La
Charte
protège
les minorités religieuses contre la menace de "tyrannie de la
majorité".

[
193
]

The Court does not hesitate to add that these
words of wisdom stated by the late Dickson J. are as keenly relevant in the
context of a secular or agnostic majority.

[
194
]

In conclusion, it is to be hoped that the
Supreme Court of Canada, in its decision in
S.L. v. Commission scolaire des
Chênes,
[50]

will clarify the roles of the State and of the parents in the education of
children.

FOR THESE
REASONS, THE COURT:

[
195
]

DISMISSES
the
Attorney General's motion for interlocutory injunction;
